verdicts.reason: Both score the presence of coordinated mass-campaign artifacts (slogans, campaign headers/metadata, standardized language) against a bespoke-independent-composition zero anchor, item for item.
A form-letter campaign submission is typically polished and standardized, so it can score high on campaign residue while scoring low on unpolished earnest personal voice, and vice versa.
Citing CFR parts and sections is a surface citation practice, while arguing the rule exceeds statutory authority is a substantive legal claim that can appear with or without any CFR citations.

X credits occupation or direct exposure with no location, whereas Y requires a named location, address, or stated distance from a facility for a high score, so an occupation-based exposure comment splits the two.
Both ask whether the comment supplies a concrete alternative regulatory design specific enough to implement, with the same zero anchor of proposing nothing.

Campaign residue tracks standardized mass-appeal language while grassroots voice tracks unedited novice prose with earnest personal stance; a slick campaign letter is high on one and low on the other.
X hinges on locational specificity such as an address or facility proximity, while Y credits any sustained first-person account of work, loss, or risk with no geographic anchor at all.

X covers corporate letterhead and high-status private signatories as well as government ones, while Y is restricted to agency or state-government template markers, so a corporate executive letter scores high on X and low on Y.

Y explicitly caps mere coalition name-dropping at 5 and reserves 10 for substance delegated to another commenter's filing, which is exactly the dense-cross-reference-but-self-arguing case X scores high.

Both score first-person direct stake through residence/ownership, occupation/work, and personal exposure to the rule against an identical purely-general zero anchor; the wording differs but the underlying concept does not.
Talking about the rulemaking process is unrelated to parroting the rule's own summary text back as the comment's content; a comment can do either without the other.
Both score paper-route provenance evidence through OCR letter-substitution damage, broken word spacing, RECEIVED/POSTMARKED stamps, and fax header junk, against clean native digital text.

Both score document-production and filing debris in the extracted text -- OCR corruption, duplicated headers/covers, page or slide extraction, and see-attached references -- against clean native prose.

X is a weak-integration penalty that scores 0 when every citation is tightly tied to a claim, while Y scores the sheer accumulation of statistics and named sources, so a rigorously sourced comment is high on Y and 0 on X.

X keys on document-wrapper markers such as letterhead and senior signatories, while Y keys on asserted scale claims like membership counts, reach, and longevity, which can appear in plain unformatted text.
Emotional intensity of register is independent of whether the writer describes their own operational practice in the regulated activity; either can occur without the other.

Y scores 0 for institutional plural voice regardless of exposure detail and requires the writer to be an unrepresented private individual, whereas X credits any sustained personal-stake account including one embedded in an organizational filing.
Both score whether the commenter supplies its own derived monetary compliance-cost figures with the basis stated, with the same no-figures zero anchor.
